content: Pruritus, commonly referred to as itching, is a sensation that compels individuals to scratch. In 8% to 15% of cases, the underlying cause of pruritus remains unknown. Chronic pruritus of unknown origin (CPUO) is a subset of generalized pruritus, with its prevalence ranging from 3.6% to 44.5%, particularly affecting older adults. When the cause of pruritus is identifiable, treatment can often be straightforward, provided there is an effective therapy for the underlying condition. However, managing CPUO is particularly challenging due to the lack of understanding of its pathophysiology. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of various interventions for CPUO in both adults and children. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Skin Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and trial registries, up to July 2019. They also reviewed reference lists of included studies to identify additional relevant trials. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized controlled trials that assessed interventions for CPUO, as defined by the International Forum for the Study of Itch (IFSI) classification. Eligible interventions included non-pharmacological treatments, topical therapies, and systemic pharmacological treatments, with comparators such as active treatments, placebos, sham procedures, or no treatment. The primary outcomes of interest were patientor parent-reported pruritus intensity and adverse events. Secondary outcomes included health-related quality of life, sleep disturbances, depression, and patient satisfaction. The certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The review found a significant lack of evidence for most interventions of interest, such as emollient creams, cooling lotions, topical corticosteroids, topical antidepressants, systemic antihistamines, systemic antidepressants, systemic anticonvulsants, and phototherapy. Only one study met the inclusion criteria. This study involved 257 participants (253 analyzed) aged 18 to 65 years, with 60.6% being female. The trial, conducted across 25 centers in the United States, investigated the safety and efficacy of three different doses of oral serlopitant (5 mg, 1 mg, and 0.25 mg) compared to placebo for severe chronic pruritus. The treatment duration was six weeks, with outcomes measured at the end of this period, except for adverse events, which were monitored throughout the study. The study was funded by a pharmaceutical company. Among the participants, 55% had CPUO, while the remaining 45% had dermatological diagnoses such as atopic dermatitis/eczema (37.3%), psoriasis (6.7%), and acne (3.6%). All participants had experienced pruritus for six weeks or longer. The total study duration was 10 weeks. Attempts to retrieve outcome data specifically for the subgroup of participants with CPUO were unsuccessful. For participants receiving serlopitant 5 mg, there was a potential improvement in patient-reported pruritus intensity, as measured by the visual analogue scale (VAS), compared to placebo (126 participants; risk ratio [RR] 2.06, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.27 to 3.35; low-certainty evidence). However, the effects of serlopitant 5 mg on adverse events, health-related quality of life (measured by the Dermatology Life Quality Index [DLQI]), and sleep disturbances (measured by the Pittsburgh Sleep Symptom Questionnaire-Insomnia [PSSQ-I]) were uncertain due to very low-certainty evidence. Adverse events were reported in 127 participants (RR 1.48, 95% CI 0.87 to 2.50), health-related quality of life showed a mean difference (MD) of -4.20 (95% CI -11.68 to 3.28), and sleep disturbances had an RR of 0.49 (95% CI 0.24 to 1.01). For participants receiving serlopitant 1 mg, there was a possible improvement in pruritus intensity compared to placebo, but the 95% CI suggested that there might be little to no difference between groups (126 participants; RR 1.50, 95% CI 0.89 to 2.54; low-certainty evidence). The effects on adverse events (128 participants; RR 1.45, 95% CI 0.86 to 2.47), health-related quality of life (DLQI; MD -6.90, 95% CI -14.38 to 0.58), and sleep disturbances (PSSQ-I; RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.84) were also uncertain due to very low-certainty evidence. For participants receiving serlopitant 0.25 mg, there was a potential improvement in pruritus intensity compared to placebo, but again, the 95% CI indicated that there might be little to no difference between groups (127 participants; RR 1.66, 95% CI 1.00 to 2.77; low-certainty evidence). The effects on adverse events (127 participants; RR 1.29, 95% CI 0.75 to 2.24), health-related quality of life (DLQI; MD -5.70, 95% CI -13.18 to 1.78), and sleep disturbances (PSSQ-I; RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.17) were similarly uncertain due to very low-certainty evidence. The most commonly reported adverse events across all groups included somnolence, diarrhea, headache, and nasopharyngitis. The study did not measure outcomes related to depression or patient satisfaction. The certainty of evidence for all outcomes was downgraded due to indirectness (only 55% of participants had CPUO) and imprecision. Additional downgrades were applied to outcomes other than patient-reported pruritus intensity due to concerns about risk of bias in the selection of reported results and missing outcome data (specifically for sleep disturbances). Overall, the risk of bias was deemed to be generally low. In conclusion, there is a lack of evidence to address the review question regarding interventions for CPUO. Most interventions of interest had no eligible studies. The neurokinin 1 receptor (NK1R) antagonist serlopitant was the only intervention assessed, with low-certainty evidence suggesting it may reduce pruritus intensity compared to placebo. However, the effects of serlopitant on other outcomes remain uncertain due to very low-certainty evidence. Further studies with larger sample sizes and a focus on patients with CPUO are needed. In the meantime, healthcare professionals, patients, and other stakeholders may need to rely on indirect evidence from studies on other forms of chronic pruritus when making treatment decisions for this condition.
